summary.text: Blood pressure is the pressure of circulating blood against the walls of blood vessels, and most of it comes from the heart pumping blood.
It is usually written as the systolic pressure, the maximum during a heartbeat, over the diastolic pressure, the minimum between heartbeats.
It is one of the vital signs that healthcare professionals use to evaluate a patient's health.

facts.label: Where measured
facts.value: Most commonly in a brachial artery

facts.label: Normal resting adult
facts.value: Under 120/80 mmHg by AHA and ACC

facts.label: Daily rhythm
facts.value: Highest in early morning and evenings, lowest at night

items.prompt: A reading is 130 over 80 mmHg. What is the gap between the two numbers called?

options.label: Mean arterial pressure
Venous pressure
Pulse pressure
Normotension

items.explain: The difference between systolic and diastolic pressure is the pulse pressure; the average over a cardiac cycle is the mean arterial pressure.

items.prompt: A patient's blood pressure no longer falls overnight the way it normally does. What does losing that fall go with?

options.label: A greater future risk of cardiovascular disease
A lower risk, since the pressure stays steady
No link to later health at all
A switch from hypertension to hypotension

items.explain: Loss of the normal fall in blood pressure at night is associated with a greater future risk of cardiovascular disease.

items.prompt: A healthy adult reads just under 90/60 but feels completely fine. In practice, is the pressure treated as too low?

options.label: Yes, any reading below that mark is dangerous
No, it counts as too low only if symptoms are present
Yes, because the diagnostic standard is exact
No, because low readings are always the healthiest

items.explain: There is no accepted diagnostic standard for hypotension; pressures below 90/60 are commonly regarded as low, but in practice pressure is considered too low only if symptoms are present.

items.prompt: In many older people the gap between the top and bottom numbers widens. What is this rise attributed to?

options.label: A thicker, slower blood supply
A weaker heartbeat
A lower blood volume
Stiffer arteries

items.explain: The rise in pulse pressure with age is attributed to increased stiffness of the arteries.

items.prompt: Pressure in the right atrium of the heart is only about 5 mmHg. How does venous pressure compare with arterial pressure?

options.label: Much lower
About the same
Much higher
Too variable to compare

items.explain: Venous pressure is much lower than arterial pressure, with common values of 5 mmHg in the right atrium and 8 mmHg in the left atrium.

items.prompt: When you stand up quickly, sensors called baroreceptors help adjust your blood pressure in the short term. Through what do they act?

options.label: The kidneys, which alone adjust the pressure
The heart valves, which open and close faster
The red blood cells, which change in number
The brain, which signals nerves and hormones

items.explain: In the short term, blood pressure is regulated by baroreceptors, which act via the brain to influence the nervous system and endocrine system.

paragraphs.heading: Push against the walls
paragraphs.text: Blood pressure is the push of circulating blood against the walls of the vessels it flows through. Most of that push comes from the heart pumping blood around the body. Used on its own, the term means the pressure in a brachial artery, which is the usual place to measure it. It generally refers to the pressure in the arteries of the systemic circulation.

paragraphs.heading: Reading the two numbers
paragraphs.text: A reading is written as two numbers: the systolic pressure, the highest point during one heartbeat, over the diastolic pressure, the lowest point between beats. The units are millimetres of mercury (mmHg) or kilopascals (kPa). The gap between the two numbers is called the pulse pressure, and the average over a whole heartbeat cycle is the mean arterial pressure. For a resting adult, the AHA and ACC call normal anything under 120/80 mmHg, the ESC uses under 120/70 mmHg, and normal also means over 90/60 mmHg.

paragraphs.heading: What moves it
paragraphs.text: Cardiac output, systemic vascular resistance, blood volume and how stiff the arteries are all influence blood pressure. It shifts with a person's situation, emotional state, activity and health, and with temperature, noise, stress, food and drink, posture, drugs and disease. Age and sex play a part too. Over short spans of time, baroreceptors regulate it, acting through the brain on the nervous system and the endocrine system.

paragraphs.heading: Too high or too low
paragraphs.text: Pressure that is consistently too high is called hypertension, pressure that is too low is hypotension, and normal pressure is normotension. Long-term hypertension raises the risk of many diseases, including stroke, heart disease and kidney failure. There is no accepted standard for hypotension, though readings under 90/60 are commonly regarded as low, and in practice pressure counts as too low only when it causes symptoms. The risk of cardiovascular disease climbs steadily once systolic pressure rises above 90 mmHg.

paragraphs.heading: A daily rhythm
paragraphs.text: Blood pressure changes from minute to minute and usually follows a 24-hour cycle, highest in the early morning and evening and lowest at night. Losing that normal fall at night is linked with a greater future risk of cardiovascular disease. Since readings vary so much, and readings from an automated device over 24 hours predict outcomes better, some authorities such as NICE in the UK prefer this ambulatory method for diagnosing hypertension.

paragraphs.heading: Changes over a lifetime
paragraphs.text: Children have lower normal ranges than adults, and these depend on their height. In adults in most societies, systolic pressure tends to rise from early adulthood up to at least age 70, while diastolic pressure starts falling earlier, around age 55. Pulse pressure rises markedly after 40, a change put down to the arteries growing stiffer. Even so, this rise with age is not considered healthy, and some isolated communities do not show it at all.
